title: Armstrong's fame, white concert trumpeters, and Johnny Dunn's challenge
summary: Barker says Armstrong stayed happy with fame, some white concert players ignored him, and tells of Johnny Dunn challenging him in Chicago.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Seeing as how Armstrong, can you hold it over here soon? Did I just want to give it a hand? Seeing as how, you know, Armstrong went up to Chicago and made a big name for himself, in a way, he sort of put himself above that, all that competitiveness and savage competition when he became famous. And I'm just wondering if, do you think he ever took his fame for granted or was he always trying to expand it?

No, he was a happy man. He, he was so acclaimed by everybody. Every trumpet player, everybody who, who, who played a horn, paid him homage somewhere or other, or they stayed a distance from him. Whole lot of great white trumpet players, legitimate trumpet players, never went near Louis. You dig, they may have looked, but they dismissed him as, not exactly black, but that kind of style, that ain't, well, that's something to do with it too, but you always, you don't always put it on being black. He could have been white and they would ignore them. They got whites who would ignore Bix in preference of Lurie or Henry Bussey or Tony, Lurie Pinnico, you dig, B.A. Rolf. There are the trumpet players who were in the concert field, like B.A. Rolf, and you heard of B.A. Rolf. Oh, I had a big band one time. And they had these guys with the Ringling Brothers Circus, great technical concert cornet players, triple tongue artisan, and play high range, you know, and, and they dismissed, they never went near Armstrong, you know, because they couldn't conceive what the hell he was playing lots of times. It was funky black music. You dig? Unless you went in the story of a hunky-tonk and see Lurie how he could captivate black people doing this thing, all whites who got the message, like the white kids today have got the message of doing all the black dances that the rocks do. It's one of them things. But Lurie never looked back to, to, to claim nothing. At the same time, Lurie, before Lurie, there was Johnny Dunn, who had this extremely long trumpet, and he used to boast, I'm the greatest trumpet player that ever lived. I'm the king of the trumpet. He was called king, Johnny Dunn, played with Mamie Smith. And so far, he went to prove he was king, he went to Chicago to challenge Lurie. And reputed to have, went to the band, said, say, hand me that horn, boy. Show you how to play that horn. And Lurie handed him the horn, and he played, and when he got through, Lurie got angry, was angry about it, and said, take your horn and blow him out of here. And Lurie just proceeded to play Tiger Rag, maybe a hundred chorus, which, Johnny Dunn probably couldn't play, maybe a half a dozen.
Was Johnny Dunn from New Orleans?

No, he's from, he was from Memphis. But he was famous around New York. He was starring Broadway shows, like Little Lesson's Blackbirds, and some of them shows, and he played extra long trumpet about three feet long. And he sat in the pit, and he blew, like for the chorus girls when they come out. It was exciting to see him stand up and blow. And there's some records you could hear him, things he did, but nothing with the technique and the power and the drive and the beauty of Armstrong.
